summary:
A visitor to Córdoba operates under Argentina's national legal framework, and nothing in the available sources records a provincial rule departing from it. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, while anti-discrimination protection runs through a combination of national and provincial statutes. The Chamber of Deputies approved the law 167-17-7 and the Senate passed it on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than repeal. Emergency Decree 62/2025, issued in February 2025, amends the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment, and Decree 61/2025 changes where transgender people are held in the prison system. Both bind Córdoba as they bind every other Argentine province. The Federación Argentina de Lesbianas, Gays, Bisexuales y Trans announced legal action, and constitutional experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the decrees unlawful and unconstitutional. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a 62% increase, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026. Of those incidents, 43% were committed by people unknown to the victims.

Security forces figure prominently in the same accounting. The observatory recorded 64 cases of institutional violence by security forces in 2025 against 17 in 2024, and 32% of all recorded incidents occurred inside police stations or prisons. Between 18 and 26 November 2025, police in Salta, Córdoba and Buenos Aires provinces intervened in the deaths of three LGBT+ people over eight days, with Córdoba's forces explicitly named in that documented pattern.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, said the national government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in that case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration across the wider legal and civic environment a visitor enters.

The national hate-crime figures place 2025 as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with Agencia Presentes describing the record annual count as such on 19 March 2026. The pattern of security-force involvement documented across Salta, Córdoba and Buenos Aires in a single eight-day window in November 2025 indicates that the institutional-violence component of that count is not concentrated in one province.
localsOnly:
Residents of Córdoba change their legal gender through the national procedure established by Law 26.743, with no surgery, hormone treatment or court order required, and provincial anti-discrimination statutes operate alongside the national ones.

Residents under 18 are the group directly affected by Emergency Decree 62/2025, which withdraws access to gender-affirming surgery and comprehensive hormonal treatment that the Gender Identity Law had made available. Transgender residents held in the provincial prison system are governed by Decree 61/2025 on placement.

Litigation challenging both decrees was announced by the Federación Argentina de Lesbianas, Gays, Bisexuales y Trans, and constitutional experts called the decrees unlawful. Residents currently detained or in the process of challenging administrative decisions stand to be affected by whatever that litigation produces.

Provincial police forces are named among the security forces that intervened in the deaths of three LGBT+ people between 18 and 26 November 2025, which is relevant to residents' dealings with Córdoba's police and to complaints of institutional violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation against Emergency Decree 62/2025 and Decree 61/2025 is unresolved in the sources available here; no judgment, injunction or procedural ruling is recorded, so the current binding status of the decrees beyond their issuance cannot be confirmed from this inventory.

Whether Decree 62/2025 or Decree 61/2025 has been applied in Córdoba in any specific instance is not sourced. No case, directive or provincial implementing measure from Córdoba appears in the inventory.

The 227 hate-crime cases recorded nationally for 2025 are not disaggregated by province in the sources available, so the share attributable to Córdoba is unresolved.

Outright International's negative assessments of 12 March 2026 are recorded as assessments only; the specific legal or administrative measures underlying them are not detailed in the inventory.

No source in this inventory addresses access to transition-related healthcare, identity-document processing times or facility availability within Córdoba province, and none is inferred here.
